## Simple explanation

Hashing turns data of varying sizes into a fixed-size value called a
hash. Hashes can support fast lookup, deduplication, and data-integrity
checks, depending on the hash function and use case.

## Technical explanation

A hash function maps input data to a fixed-size output. Different inputs
can share an output (a collision), so collision handling is essential
for data structures. Cryptographic hash functions have additional
security properties and should not be confused with ordinary hash
functions used for indexing.

## Why it matters in AI engineering

Hashing can index features, identify duplicate files, partition data,
or support privacy-preserving workflows. Hash choice must match the
application; ordinary hashes are not suitable for password storage or
cryptographic integrity guarantees.

## How it works

The function processes an input and deterministically produces a
fixed-size value. Hash tables use that value to select a storage
location, resolving collisions when different keys map to the same
location. Cryptographic hashes are designed to make certain attacks
computationally difficult.

## Practical example

A data pipeline can hash file contents to identify exact duplicate
images before building a training dataset. Near-duplicate images
require similarity methods rather than exact hashes.

## Common misconceptions

- Hashing is not encryption; it is generally not designed to be
  reversible.
- Hash collisions are possible.
- A fast general-purpose hash is not automatically secure for
  cryptographic uses.
